title: Variables and Data Types
subtitle: Store information and work with Python
description: Learn variables, strings, integers, floats, booleans, type conversion and how Python handles different kinds of values.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand Variables and Data Types

Welcome to Lesson 2: Variables and Data Types. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Variables and Data Types”. The goal is to store information and work with Python. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
A variable gives a meaningful name to a value that a program needs to remember. Names such as learnerName, score, and isComplete communicate purpose better than vague names such as x or data.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Python. Paste this snippet into the Python editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Variables and Data Types in practice

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Store information and work with Python. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A setting must never be reassigned during the program. What should you choose?
options: A constant or immutable binding supported by the language.
A global variable that any function can change.
A string containing the setting name.
A loop that resets the value repeatedly.
blocks.explanation: Constants communicate intent and help prevent accidental reassignment.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Constants communicate intent and help prevent accidental reassignment.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Constants communicate intent and help prevent accidental reassignment.

blocks.title: Sample 2: Variables and Data Types in practice

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real Python project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A field may not exist in an incoming user profile. Which implementation is safest?
options: Assume the field always exists.
Use the missing value in arithmetic immediately.
Check for absence and apply a meaningful fallback or validation error.
Replace every missing value with zero without checking its meaning.
blocks.explanation: Missing, unknown, and zero are not interchangeable; handle absence according to the requirement.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Missing, unknown, and zero are not interchangeable; handle absence according to the requirement.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Missing, unknown, and zero are not interchangeable; handle absence according to the requirement.

blocks.text: Types describe which values are allowed and which operations make sense. Some languages check many types before running; others allow more flexibility at runtime, but in every language the developer must still reason about missing, malformed, or unexpected values.

blocks.title: Sample 3: Variables and Data Types in practice

blocks.question: A program stores “25” from a text field and needs to add 5 points. What should happen first?
options: Concatenate arbitrary values until the result looks right.
Use the value as a number without checking it.
Convert it only after a crash.
Parse and validate the text as a number before calculating.
blocks.explanation: Input text should be parsed and validated before numeric operations.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Input text should be parsed and validated before numeric operations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Input text should be parsed and validated before numeric operations.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning

Use a constant for a value that should not be reassigned and a variable for state that legitimately changes. Keep values close to where they are used and avoid maintaining duplicate copies that can drift out of sync.

blocks.text: Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Learn variables, strings, integers, floats, booleans, type conversion and how Python handles different kinds of values. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: Two screens keep separate copies of a learner’s progress and now disagree. What is the best fix?
options: Keep changing both copies manually.
Use one source of truth and derive the display values from it.
Choose whichever screen looks newer.
Store the progress in the screen title.
blocks.explanation: Duplicated mutable state often becomes inconsistent; derive displays from one reliable value.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Duplicated mutable state often becomes inconsistent; derive displays from one reliable value.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Duplicated mutable state often becomes inconsistent; derive displays from one reliable value.

blocks.question: A learner’s XP changes after every correct answer. Which design is easiest to maintain?
options: Repeat the current XP number in many places.
Store XP in one appropriately scoped variable and update it deliberately.
Use a different variable name for every update.
Convert XP to a text label before doing arithmetic.
blocks.explanation: One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. One well-defined source of truth prevents values from drifting apart.
